Ukraine’s Zelenskiy escalates criticism of SpaceX over speed caps

Reuters

14 November, 2026 08:00 pm IST

KYIV, Nov 14 (Reuters) – Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskiy escalated his criticism of SpaceX on Saturday, saying speed restrictions on its military-grade Starshield satellite terminals had dangerous political implications and undermined critical air defences.

Zelenskiy said Starshield terminals operating in temporarily Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine had been limited to a maximum speed of 161 kph for the past five days, hampering Ukraine’s military capabilities.

The Ukrainian Defence Ministry has raised the issue with SpaceX at the institutional level, Zelenskiy said.

Show Full Article

“The restrictions have now been in place for five days. They say it is some kind of technical issue. We do not believe that is the case,” Zelenskiy told reporters in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

“If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporarily occupied territories as not ours. And that is why I believe we have the right to raise this issue and restore the speed – so that there are no restrictions at all.”

Zelenskiy said the speed restrictions made it more difficult for Ukrainian air defence units to intercept Russian jet-powered drones and made Ukrainian cities more vulnerable. He said he had ordered his top military and foreign ministry officials to address the issue and seek clarification.

SpaceX has pushed back against the allegations, denying that it introduced new restrictions or made any changes to its satellite operations.

It is the second such outage in recent weeks. In mid-October, Ukrainian officials said that SpaceX limited the speed of Starlink and its Starshield communication systems to about 160 kph (100 mph) amid tensions with US President Donald Trump’s administration over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Service was then restored on October 24.

(Reporting by Olena Harmash; Editing by Hugh Lawson)

US floated idea of Ukraine ceding Donbas for NATO membership, Zelenskiy says

14 November, 2026 06:00 pm IST

By Olena Harmash KYIV, Nov 14 (Reuters) – US negotiators have floated the idea of Ukraine’s potential withdrawal from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, following the latest round of peace talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi.

This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised during the talks, Zelenskiy said in remarks to reporters released by his office on Saturday.

“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?” he said.

Show Full Article

“That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda. But you have also heard (Russian President Vladimir) Putin’s signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation.”

Putin has long said Ukrainian membership of NATO is a red line for Moscow, citing the issue as one reason for launching Russia’s full-blown invasion in 2022.

Zelenskiy reiterated his position that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory but said that if it received a comprehensive package including security guarantees, the right to a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to a national referendum.

‘THIS WAR MUST BE ENDED FIRST’

Echoing comments made by European leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, Zelenskiy dismissed Russia’s call for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before the specifics are agreed on how to end the war in Ukraine.

“We cannot turn everything upside down and start by talking about changing the security framework in the world or across the continent overall, and only then talk about ending this war. This war must be ended first,” he said.

Zelenskiy also dismissed Putin’s suggestion for a local humanitarian ceasefire in Kostiantynivka, a hotly contested city in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, saying it reflected Moscow’s inability to take the city by force. Civilians there have already had the opportunity to evacuate, he added.

“Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way,” he said.

Ukraine has given a list of seven or eight other frontline settlements where civilians, including children, are trapped for a potential humanitarian truce but Russia prefers to use them as military targets, Zelenskiy said.

Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians in the war.

LARGE PRISONER EXCHANGE AGREED

The two days of US-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia concluded on Wednesday in the Emirati capital without a major breakthrough, though the sides agreed to a prisoner exchange that will involve more than 1,000 people, Zelenskiy said.

The final numbers for the prisoner swap were still under discussion, he added.

US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had pledged to raise an energy ceasefire with Putin at a meeting in Moscow on Thursday, Zelenskiy said, but there was no news of any progress after their talks.

“Putin personally does not support a ceasefire,” he said.

Zelenskiy met Witkoff and Kushner on Thursday in Ireland after their talks in Moscow. He said the US negotiators had told him that all sides had agreed for Europe to have a seat at the negotiating table in forthcoming peace talks.

In Abu Dhabi, delegates from Europe — which is now Ukraine’s largest financial and military backer — had talks with US and Ukrainian officials but did not sit at the table with Russia.

At the summit in Ireland, EU leaders agreed that Europe’s team for any Ukraine peace talks would comprise five major military powers — non-EU member Britain plus France, Germany, Italy and Poland — as well as EU officials.

(Reporting by Olena Harmash; Editing by Daniel Flynn and Gareth Jones)

Analysis-A new ‘Yalta’? Trump and Putin push for a meeting that Xi is wary of hosting

Reuters

Follow Us:

By Trevor Hunnicutt, Mei Mei Chu and Andrew Osborn WASHINGTON/BEIJING/MOSCOW, Nov 14 (Reuters) – The world’s three most powerful leaders could sit down together next week to discuss global flashpoints, from wars in Ukraine and Iran to nuclear weapons and artificial intelligence.

The prospects for any grand bargain emerging from the rare encounter, however, are slim.

Down-to-the-wire negotiations over a meeting between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin have not yet yielded an agenda or format for talks, according to two people familiar with the planning. But a meeting is expected in Shenzhen, where the leaders will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, the people said.

Show Full Article

The three men come with very different goals.

Putin sees a chance to secure an agreement to end the war in Ukraine on his terms. Trump — battered by his Republican Party’s recent electoral losses — sees a moment for the history books, with possible movement toward a three-way agreement on nuclear arms control.

For Xi, however, it is an unpredictable gathering full of risks.

The Republican president’s improvisational style clashes with Xi’s scripted approach to high-profile events. And Trump’s hope for arms control rubs against the reality that China — which has far fewer nuclear weapons than the US or Russia — considers itself a nuclear underdog.

“This is something the Chinese hate,” said Edgard Kagan, a former senior Biden White House official for East Asia now with the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a think tank. “I think it’s fair to say the Chinese do not want arms control discussions with the United States. And they certainly don’t want to do it with the United States and Russia, because it suggests that they accept the framing that they are now a major nuclear power that should be subject to similar restrictions.”

For smaller governments not at the table, including Ukraine and Taiwan, the idea of the big powers possibly cutting a private deal without them is a cause of deep unease.

The meeting would be Trump’s latest in a series of diplomatic spectacles over his nearly six years as US president, including his prior meetings with Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. None of those meetings produced a breakthrough.

A senior Trump administration official said “we do not expect to get to any kind of agreement” on nuclear issues but added “it’s time for China to sort of step up” and talk about the topic.

“China is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state,” said a spokesperson for Beijing’s embassy in Washington on Friday. “We have nothing to share at the moment.”

Russia’s embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.

SOME NATIONS FEAR A NEW ‘YALTA’ CONFERENCE

The proposed meeting has drawn comparisons, particularly in Russia, with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the US, Britain and the Soviet Union that formalized spheres of influence, set the stage for the post-World War Two order and became shorthand for great-power deals imposed on smaller countries.

For Russian nationalists, the prospect of an updated version of Yalta has generated excitement, potentially opening the door to an agreement to end the four-year-old Ukraine conflict in a manner that would favor Moscow.

Just holding the meeting elevates Russia to the status of a superpower alongside China and the US, they say.

“It shows who is important in the world: We are, China and the West,” Russian nationalist ideologue Alexander Dugin told Radio Sputnik this week. “It’s deeply symbolic — it’s a confirmation of a multi-polar world that the West denies.”

But the possible meeting has generated anxiety from Kyiv to Tokyo, according to people briefed on those governments’ reactions.

“We really don’t want this to turn into ‘Yalta 2, 3, 4,’ with a redistribution of influence,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said last month.

The optics are awkward for China, which was not invited in 1945 and tries to present itself as an advocate for smaller countries.

A RELUCTANT HOST

Trump’s suggestion of nuclear talks is a nonstarter for Beijing, said Chinese academics interviewed by Reuters. Russia and the United States each possess more than 5,000 nuclear warheads, while China has around 500, although Beijing is rapidly expanding its arsenal.

Still, next week Xi will play host. Beijing and Moscow have grown closer in recent years, trading oil and gas and military know-how. But they have taken different approaches to the potential trilateral meeting.

While Moscow sought a conversation on the war in Ukraine, Beijing has resisted putting that topic on the agenda, according to one of the people briefed on the meeting and a European diplomat, both speaking on the condition of anonymity. A US official said on Friday that Trump was not likely to raise the war in Ukraine and that three-way talks were not the proper forum to do so.

“Suggestions are being exchanged regarding a possible agenda,” Dmitry Peskov, Putin’s spokesman, told reporters on Monday. “In any case, the meeting will certainly be interesting. And, of course, it will capture the attention of people all over the world.”

That is also Trump’s hope.

Facing a Democratic-controlled Congress next year, he may be seeking wins abroad. An agreement on arms or help ending the war with Iran could burnish his legacy.

“The president will undoubtedly be seeking to use this trip to reassert leadership, authority, demonstrate his statesmanship capabilities, and essentially show off on the international stage,” said Kurt Tong, a former senior State Department official dealing with East Asia, now a managing partner at the Asia Group consultancy.

(Reporting by Trevor Hunnicutt in Washington, Mei Mei Chu in Beijing and Andrew Osborn in Moscow; Additional reporting by David Brunnstrom, Andrea Shalal and Joe Cash; Editing by Don Durfee and Sanjeev Miglani)

Year after curbs on content takedown powers, Centre weighs allowing junior cops to probe cybercrime

Section 78 of IT Act bars officers below Inspector rank from investigating offences under the law. Centre's high-level committee on digital arrest scams has backed amending the law.

New Delhi: The central government’s high-level committee on digital arrest scams has backed amending the Information Technology Act to let police officers below the rank of Inspector investigate specified cybercrime offences. The minutes, however, do not specify which offences would be covered.

The proposal has been recorded in the minutes of the inter-departmental committee’s 24 September meeting, chaired by the Special Secretary (Internal Security) in the Union Home Ministry. The minutes are annexed to the ministry’s fifth status report to the Supreme Court—seen by ThePrint—filed on 7 October in a suo motu case on digital arrest scams.

Section 78 of the IT Act bars any officer below Inspector rank from investigating offences under the law.

Show Full Article

This proposal comes a year after the IT ministry—in October 2025—amended the IT Rules, so that only police officers of Deputy Inspector General rank or above could issue content takedown notices to platforms.

The 24 September minutes state that the “limited availability of officers of the required rank, particularly Inspectors in specialised cybercrime units, may create an operational bottleneck if the number of FIRs increases substantially”. The committee “considered the need of the suitable amendment”, under which officers “below the present prescribed rank may be empowered to investigate specified cybercrime offences”.

The committee has sought data from I4C, the Union home ministry and the Union IT ministry, so that it can examine “the feasibility of empowering suitably trained officers of lower rank, subject to appropriate safeguards and qualifications”. I4C is an initiative of the Ministry of Home Affairs linked to cybercrime that became an attached office of the ministry in July 2024.

Also Read: Meta tells govt it acted on 61k ‘inciteful posts’ in 2 weeks; claims 95% drop in AI content on platforms

Why the change The trigger behind the proposal is the e-Zero FIR system, which automatically converts large cybercrime complaints into FIRs. According to the minutes of the panel’s meeting, it has raised the share of complaints registered as FIRs from one-two percent to about eight percent.

The offences covered under IT Act range from hacking and identity theft, to publishing or transmitting “obscene” material online under Section 67, a provision police have also invoked over social media posts. Parliament last changed the rank requirement in 2008, lowering it from Deputy Superintendent of Police to Inspector. Several High Courts have, over time , held that IT Act investigations by officers below Inspector rank do not meet the law’s requirement.

Immigration data & bank checks The status report details several other measures being undertaken.

The Central Bureau of Investigation’s report, annexed to the filing, says the agency met the Bureau of Immigration “for using the immigration travel database to curb misuse of international roaming connections operated from scam compounds abroad”. It adds that the “technical feasibility of sharing said information was discussed”. CBI presents the talks as a follow-up to its national cyber-crime conference in February this year.

At a 22 July meeting with the Department of Financial Services, and banks’ chief vigilance and technology officers, CBI secured agreement on several steps.

Every bank account is to be linked to the holder’s Aadhaar-verified mobile number. Biometric OTP checks are to be extended to the opening of accounts in all banks. Mule-account databases are to be shared among banks in real time, and the Reserve Bank of India’s AI tool, MuleHunter.AI, is to be strengthened “with IP logs and geolocation data”.

Telecom checks The Department of Telecommunications told the court in October that on 17 August, it directed telecom operators to block SIM cards issued beyond the legal limit.

Operators are to use a “table of mobile connections and images” made available to them on DoT’s Digital Intelligence Platform, and have until 30 November to comply. I4C also shares with DoT, every day, the mobile numbers reported by complainants on the national cybercrime portal. Operators are to deploy AI and machine-learning tools to “red flag suspect connections, to re-verify them in a time bound manner and to disconnect those which fail verification”.

The home ministry status report submitted in court also records a rise in grievances from account holders, whose bank accounts were frozen, or whose money was held during cybercrime investigations. They went from about 2,000 in May, to 93,041 by 30 September. In a May letter to state police chiefs, I4C said many grievances were being closed “with inadequate or unreasonable remarks”.

Another 983 petitions seeking to unfreeze accounts are pending in high courts. The petitioners include the stock-broking platform Groww, fintech firms such as RapiPay and Resilient Innovations—the company behind BharatPe—and small businesses and individuals.

The Supreme Court will hear the case next on 23 November.

(Edited by Mannat Chugh)
